title: Two preferences between linguistic time and ESG
affiliations: SOAS University of London, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law and Soochow University

detail.title: Two preferences between linguistic time and ESG
detail.abstract: We examine the influence of linguistic factors on firm ESG preferences, specifically focusing on the impact of language on ESG behavior. Using a comprehensive cross-country sample of 49,026 firm-year observations from 61 countries spanning 2003 to 2020, we find that strong FTR languages negatively correlate with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance. Speakers of strong FTR languages tend to have more precise perceptions of timing, which correlates with lower ESG preferences. Further analyses reveal that firms in countries with stronger formal institutions tend to invest less in ESG activities. This study offers a novel perspective, suggesting that companies in countries where strong-FTR languages are the official or working language exhibit a lesser future orientation and perform worse in future-oriented activities such as ESG than those in weak-FTR language environments. Our findings indicate that the language corporations use is a critical cultural variable and a strong predictor of ESG preference.

title: Overtime and Upward Earnings Management: Evidence from Chinese Firms
affiliations: Shandong Normal University, Qilu University of Technology and Qilu University of Technology

detail.title: Overtime and Upward Earnings Management: Evidence from Chinese Firms
detail.abstract: Overtime work is widespread in modern firms, yet its implications for financial reporting remain underexplored. Using a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2024, we find that greater overtime intensity is associated with higher levels of upward earnings management. We further identify two underlying mechanisms. First, the financial pressure channel suggests that high overtime intensity weakens firms' internal cash flow conditions, thereby increasing debt-servicing pressure and reinvestment constraints, particularly under high external performance expectations. Second, the incentive distortion channel suggests that overtime compresses compensation structures and weakens incentive effectiveness, thereby strengthening managerial incentives for opportunistic reporting, particularly in firms with severe agency conflicts. The effect is more pronounced among growth-stage firms and those with persistently high overtime intensity. Moreover, while such behavior may temporarily delay risk realization, it is associated with a significantly higher likelihood of future stock price crashes. Overall, we provide new evidence on how overtime practices affect financial reporting quality and highlight the tension between short-term performance pressures and long-term corporate sustainability.

title: From Text to Faces: A Systematic Review of Stable Diffusion in Facial Image Generation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Text to Faces: A Systematic Review of Stable Diffusion in Facial Image Generation
detail.abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have substantially expanded the capabilities of text-to-image synthesis, with Generative Adversarial Networks and, more recently, diffusion-based architectures such as Stable Diffusion playing a central role. While these models have enabled unprecedented realism across domains ranging from digital art to immersive virtual environments, the generation of high-fidelity facial images from textual descriptions continues to pose significant challenges. Ambiguous linguistic cues, the structural complexity of human faces, and sensitivity to extrinsic factors such as illumination and pose still limit the reliability of current approaches, particularly in high-stakes contexts including forensics and public safety. This systematic literature review investigates the current landscape of face generation using Stable Diffusion, synthesizing methodological advances, architectural adaptations, evaluation frameworks, and dataset characteristics across twelve peer-reviewed studies. Through a rigorously designed review protocol, the study identifies converging research themes and traces how the field is evolving in response to demands for personalization, controllability, and cross-modal consistency. Although recent innovations demonstrate the growing sophistication of gaze-conditioned and identity-adaptive generation, several open questions remain regarding efficiency, data diversity, and robustness under operational constraints. By mapping these developments and unresolved gaps, this review provides a comprehensive foundation for future research and highlights the considerable—yet still maturing—potential of diffusion models in applications that depend on reliable facial image synthesis.

title: Smart Industries, Smarter Energy? The impact of AI on industrial energy consumption in India
affiliations: Central University of Haryana and Central University of Haryana

detail.title: Smart Industries, Smarter Energy? The impact of AI on industrial energy consumption in India
detail.abstract: Industrial expansion elevates energy demand as it requires substantial energy input for the production and operational efficiency. Simultaneously, the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in industries is further intensifying the demand for energy. This study examines the relationship between energy consumption and industrialization and investigates the moderating role played of artificial intelligence in this nexus. This study uses India’s time series data from 1993-2023. Based on ARDL estimations, the outcomes suggest that increased use of AI reduces overall energy demand in India. However, the industrial application of AI, exhibiting the moderating effect, is found to increase the energy demand in India. Also, AI uni-directionally granger causes industrialization in India. Further, this study recommends development of green industrial framework and focus on reducing energy intensity among MSMEs. As per the authors’ knowledge, this is the first study that investigates the impact of AI adoption in Industries on energy consumption in Indian context.

title: The Specialization Inflection Theory (SIT): Beyond Adam Smith - A New Framework for Understanding When Specialization Transitions from Asset to Liability

detail.title: The Specialization Inflection Theory (SIT): Beyond Adam Smith - A New Framework for Understanding When Specialization Transitions from Asset to Liability
detail.abstract: Adam Smith’s theory of the division of labor (1776) has long served as the foundational prescription for economic productivity through specialization. Prior critiques of this theory have identified its limitations but have failed to answer the central question left open by the literature: under what conditions, exactly, does specialization transition from an individual asset to an individual liability? This paper introduces the Specialization Inflection Theory (SIT), an original theoretical framework proposing that every worker faces a specialization inflection point - a threshold beyond which continued narrowing of skill focus produces diminishing career returns and rising vulnerability. SIT posits that this inflection point is determined by three measurable variables: Task Routinizability (TR), Industry Velocity (IV), and Career Stage (CS). The paper develops SIT in dialogue with Smith (1776), Becker and Murphy (1992), Autor, Levy, and Murnane (2003), and the T-shaped skills literature, positioning it as the first conditional theory of individual specialization that generates testable predictions. It also addresses the two-level distinction, organizational versus individual, that prior critiques raised but did not formalize. The paper concludes that Smith’s theory is not wrong but incomplete: it describes the organizational optimum without modeling the individual inflection.
